     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"
     23	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Operations
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs, unless the user gives the values and asks you to treat them as given (see Critical Rules). Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window. For a performance verdict, include the side-by-side limits table from [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#limits-table-for-performance-verdicts) and the recent history (alarm history, modification history, earlier occurrences of the same pattern).
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation:
     96	
     97	- Only the recorded symptoms, findings, observations and gaps reach the investigation summary. Text in a chat message or a later mitigation plan does not, so put the verdict and the recommendation in the findings.
     98	- Write the symptom with its impact: the alarm name, threshold and breaching datapoints, whether the alarm has actions, and the onset time.
     99	- Write the root cause finding description as a complete answer on its own, in this order:
     100	  1. "Binding layer: `<layer>`." in those words.
     101	  2. The numbers that prove it: the exceeded checks (minutes at 1), per-volume demand against the volume limit, and the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes against the instance EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, for example "500 IOPS x 256 KiB = 125 MiB/s, the provisioned throughput".
     102	  3. The recent history: alarm episodes, modification history, and whether earlier peaks stopped at the same ceiling.
     103	  4. "Recommendation (proposal, not executed; it runs only after an operator approves it on the approval card):" the exact command with the target, how the target was computed, the next limit after the change, and the EBS baseline of the next larger instance size when the instance becomes the next limit.
     104	  Do not leave the conclusion or the target only under Gaps or in a later message.
     105	- Record each piece of evidence as an observation and link every observation that supports a finding to it, so each finding shows its supporting observations. This includes the limits table, the instance layer check, the volume status result and the history.
     106	- Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding. Leave out AWS FIS experiments, AWS CloudTrail events and alarms on resources that are not attached to the instance.
     107	- Link a gap only to the findings it affects. Record a gap that applies to the whole answer once.
     108	
     109	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, keep it as the verdict and write "Binding layer: Indeterminate" with the answer to the user's question first. Then present a short list of candidate causes, as described in [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#indeterminate-candidate-causes). For each candidate, give the supporting observations with numbers and the specific check that would confirm it or rule it out. Merge overlapping candidates, and name a candidate that the data rules out as ruled out, with the numbers. Do not name AWS-side impairment as the cause, and do not call the pattern an impairment pattern. Give the customer the detailed performance statistics step from [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) to run during the symptom.
     110	
     111	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     112	
     113	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     114	
     115	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     116	
     117	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     118	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The answer says "Binding layer:" followed by the layer, and gives the four exceeded checks as minutes at 1 or "no datapoints". A performance verdict has the limits table: per-volume demand next to the volume limit, summed demand of all attached volumes next to the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS, which one binds, and the exact target with its computation.
     119	- A performance verdict states the recent history: the alarm history, the modification history (latest record and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or a Gap), and whether the same pattern happened earlier.
     120	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     121	- An Indeterminate verdict says "Binding layer: Indeterminate", answers the user's question first, and lists the candidate causes, each with its supporting observations and the check that confirms or rules it out, without overlapping candidates or the same gap repeated under each one.
     122	- In an investigation, the root cause finding (or, for Indeterminate, the first finding) carries the verdict, the numbers, the history and the Recommendation, because only findings reach the summary.
     123	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first. The first lines of a snapshot answer name every snapshot with its tier and the evidence for it.
     124	- Every proposed change follows [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals): exact command, expected effect, modifications left in the 24-hour window, rollback, and the approval statement.
     125	- When a volume modification is in progress, the answer states the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window, each one completing before the next, and the count used from AWS CloudTrail or a Gap.
     126	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     127	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     128	
     129	---
     130	
     131	## Critical Rules
     132	
     133	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, key changes, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval, and the reply says so in those words whenever the user types an approval. Each proposal also gives the exact AWS CLI command the customer can run with their own credentials. See [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals).
     134	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     135	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first. Do not end the turn with a question tool or a request to pick a value: give the recommended proposal, and the command for any value the user named, then say the user can choose.
     136	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     137	- **Given facts stay given.** When the user supplies the values and asks you to treat them as given, reason from those values only. Do not query the account for other resources, and do not mix account data into the given facts. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs.
     138	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     139	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     140	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     141	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     142	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     143	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. State this rule in the answer whenever a modification is in progress or proposed.
     144	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     145	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     146	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     147	
     148	## Gotchas
     149	
     150	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     151	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     152	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     153	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     154	- When the instance is the binding layer, do not call the volume saturated, even when its idle time is near 0. Say that its I/O is waiting on the instance limit.
     155	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     156	- `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`, `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, and no datapoints is not the same as 0. The instance checks `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with `InstanceId`.
     157	- Amazon EBS detailed performance statistics are read on the instance, not through an AWS API. They are a step the customer runs; the agent never runs them.
     158	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     159	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     160	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     161	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     162	
     163	## Error Handling
     164	
     165	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     166	
     167	## References
     168	
     169	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     170	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     171	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     172	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     173	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     174	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     175	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     176	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     177	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     178	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     179	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "7d916894-5792-4712-9f29-6604d66db52e", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_444T96ghHiKgUEPGEIFe8S", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history with `DescribeAlarmHistory` for the last 24 hours: when it first entered ALARM, and any earlier ALARM and OK transitions. Report earlier transitions as history, because they show whether the pattern recurs.
     17	- Describe the impact in the symptom: the alarm name, metric, threshold, the datapoints that breached it, whether the alarm has actions configured, and the onset (the minute the metric left its normal level, for example "queue length rose from about 0 at `<time>` to 1.5 from `<time>`").
     18	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     19	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     20	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     21	
     22	### Step 2: Build the context
     23	
     24	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     25	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     26	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     27	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     28	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence.      57	An Indeterminate verdict is a short list of candidate causes, not a single sentence. The Binding layer stays Indeterminate, and the answer says so in those words: "Binding layer: Indeterminate".

     66

     73	
     74	- Percentage of each limit in use (measured IOPS and MiB/s against the volume and the instance limits).
     75	- Time per I/O from queue length and IOPS (Little's law): time per I/O in ms = average queue length / IOPS x 1,000.      5	## Elastic Volumes rules
     6	
     7	- You can make up to 4 modifications to a volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change).
     8	- Size can only increase. It cannot be reduced. To get a smaller volume, create a new volume and copy the data.
     9	- A modification request cannot be cancelled after it is submitted.
     10	- States are `modifying`, then `optimizing`, then `completed` (or `failed`). In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies, and performance is between the source and the target. The modification completes on its own.

     15	## Instance EBS layer
     16	
     17	- All volumes attached to an instance share the instance's EBS bandwidth, IOPS and throughput. Sum the measured values across all attached volumes, including the root volume.
     18	- Size any target within the instance's EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, not its burst maximum.
     19	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s at 128 KiB I/O and IOPS at 16 KiB I/O. Convert MB/s to MiB/s before comparing with volume throughput.

     23	
     24	- Amazon EBS quotas are per Region. Check each Region the user works in.
     25	- Discover quota codes by name with `ListServiceQuotas --service-code ebs`. Never hardcode quota codes.
     26	- Read defaults from the Amazon EBS quotas page. For example, the default for snapshots per Region is 100,000 and it is adjustable.

     31	
     32	- Snapshots are incremental. Deleting a snapshot might not reduce storage cost, because later snapshots can reference its blocks. Any savings figure is an upper bound.

     3	Use this file for any judgement about whether a volume or an instance is at a limit. Read the provisioned values from the APIs (`DescribeVolumes`, `DescribeInstanceTypes`). The numbers below are the documented service limits, not targets. Throughput is always in MiB/s.
     4	
     5	## Which dimension binds, by volume type
     6	
     7	| Type | Included or baseline | Maximum per volume | Ratio rules | Burst model | How to judge |
     8	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
     9	| gp3 | 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s included at any size | 80,000 IOPS; 2,000 MiB/s | Up to 500 IOPS per GiB; up to 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS | No burst | Compare actual IOPS to `Iops` AND actual MiB/s to `Throughput`. Either can bind. For a sequential workload, check throughput first |
     10	| gp2 | 3 IOPS per GiB, minimum 100 | 16,000 IOPS (reached at 5,334 GiB) | Size sets performance | Bursts to 3,000 IOPS while `BurstBalance` is above 0 | Compare actual IOPS to the baseline for the size. Check `BurstBalance` draining or at 0 |

Throughput limit = 0.256 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS, up to 4,000 MiB/s (reached at 16,000 IOPS or higher) | No burst | Compare actual IOPS to `Iops` AND actual MiB/s to the throughput limit computed from `Iops`. Either can bind |
     12	| io1 | Provisioned `Iops` | 64,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s. Up to 64,000 IOPS on Nitro-based instances; up to 32,000 IOPS on other instances | Up to 50 IOPS per GiB. Above 32,000 provisioned IOPS: 16 KiB per provisioned IOPS, so 1,000 MiB/s at 64,000 IOPS | No burst | Compare actual IOPS to `Iops` AND actual MiB/s to the throughput limit for the provisioned IOPS. Either can bind |
     13	| st1 | 40 MiB/s per TiB baseline | 500 MiB/s | Burst 250 MiB/s per TiB | `BurstBalance` | Compare MiB/s to the baseline and burst for the size; check `BurstBalance` |
     14	| sc1 | 12 MiB/s per TiB baseline | 250 MiB/s | Burst 80 MiB/s per TiB | `BurstBalance` | Compare MiB/s to the baseline and burst for the size; check `BurstBalance` |
     15	
     16	The io1 and io2 values above are from the Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes page in Sources. Throughput on io1 and io2 is not provisioned separately; the limit follows from the provisioned IOPS as shown. Do not quote any other maximum from memory.
     17	
     18	## Metric rules that change the verdict
     19	
     20	- `VolumeThroughputPercentage` exists only for Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes. It reports the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered, not MiB/s. Never use it as a throughput signal on io1 or io2. A healthy io2 volume can read 100% while its MiB/s is low.
     21	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. For io1 and io2, compute the throughput limit from the provisioned IOPS with the rules in the table.
     22	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both the `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` dimensions and exist only for Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 to get MiB/s.
     23	- `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` and `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` also use the `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` dimensions and exist only for Nitro instances. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, which is not the same as 0.
     24	- `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with the `InstanceId` dimension, on Nitro instances that are not bare metal.
     25	- `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only.
     26	- `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds. Average latency in ms per operation = Sum(time) / Sum(ops) x 1,000.
     27	- A 1-minute average hides sub-minute peaks. If the minute average is below a limit but latency and queue length rise, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` and `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` at 1 show a burst within the minute; the detailed performance statistics in troubleshoot-performance.md show it at up to 1-second granularity.

     29	## Latency expectations (documented only)
     30	
     31	| Type | Documented expectation |
     32	|---|---|
     33	| gp3 | Single-digit millisecond latency |
     34	| io2 Block Express | Under 500 microseconds average latency for 16 KiB I/O |
     35	
     36	For other types the public documentation does not give a latency number. Compare the volume against its own history in the same window on a normal day and against the type's documented expectation above.

     39	
     40	The drafts carried latency bands (for example "io2 below 1 ms, gp3 below 2 ms, st1 below 10 ms"), a queue length rule ("1 per 1,000 provisioned IOPS"), `VolumeIdleTime` bands, `BurstBalance` bands and percentage triggers ("below 95%", "above 90% of provisioned"). {"id": "477eb7eaf88942b196c8dca743aed183", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The binding limit is throughput, not IOPS. vol-0123456789abcdef0 (gp3, 20 GiB, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_5 as /dev/sdg) is set to the gp3 baseline: 3000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s. Starting around 18:07 UTC, the batch job has done sequential reads only, in 256 KiB requests. Throughput has stayed flat at exactly 125.07 MiB/s (7.87e9 bytes per minute, above the 6e9 alarm threshold) while using only about 500 IOPS. With 256 KiB requests, 125 MiB/s works out to about 500 IOPS, so the volume reaches its throughput cap long before its IOPS cap. That is why IOPS looks normal and the read rate is perfectly flat. The queue length of about 1.5 (higher than 1) shows requests waiting at that limit. The instance is not the bottleneck: its EBSReadBytes matches the volume, and EBSByteBalance% and EBSIOBalance% stayed at 99% the whole time. The fix is to raise the gp3 Throughput setting with ec2 ModifyVolume, online with no detach. For example, go to 250–500 MiB/s, leave IOPS at 3000, and keep size at 20 GiB. gp3 allows up to 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS, so 3000 IOPS supports up to 750 MiB/s. Two caveats: (1) c6i.xlarge has an EBS baseline of about 1250 Mbps (~149 MiB/s), with bursts up to 10 Gbps. Above roughly 150 MiB/s of sustained throughput, the instance becomes the cap once its EBS burst balance runs out. For sustained high rates, use a larger instance, such as c6i.2xlarge or bigger. (2) After a modification, the next one on the same volume has to wait about 6 hours. Increasing I/O size or IOPS would not help, because throughput is the limit.
## Evidence
- ec2 DescribeVolumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is gp3, Size 20 GiB, Iops 3000, Throughput 125 MiB/s, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_5 at /dev/sdg.
- CloudWatch alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes went to ALARM at 2026-11-23 18:11:18 UTC: VolumeReadBytes Sum per 60 s was 7.8688e9, 7.8688e9 and 7.8690e9, above the 6e9 threshold (7.8688e9/60 s ≈ 125 MiB/s).
- AWS/EBS metrics, 18:10–19:25 UTC, 5-minute periods: (VolumeReadBytes+VolumeWriteBytes)/period was 125.07 MiB/s in every interval, exactly the provisioned limit.
- Same window: (VolumeReadOps+VolumeWriteOps)/period was about 500 IOPS, roughly 17% of the 3000 provisioned. VolumeWriteOps and VolumeWriteBytes were 0.
- Average read size (VolumeReadBytes/VolumeReadOps) was 256 KiB (large sequential reads), so 125 MiB/s ÷ 256 KiB ≈ 500 IOPS.
- VolumeQueueLength averaged about 1.5–2.05 the whole time, showing I/O waiting at the throughput cap.
- AWS/EC2, i-1234567890abcdef0_5 (c6i.xlarge): EBSReadBytes ≈ 125.07 MiB/s, the same as the volume. EBSByteBalance% and EBSIOBalance% had a minimum of 99% from 18:00 to 19:30, so the instance EBS limit was not binding.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0
- i-1234567890abcdef0_5
- example-b-gp3-read-bytes

", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "**Throughput is the limit, not IOPS.** vol-0123456789abcdef0 is pinned at its provisioned 125 MiB/s. The fix is to raise the gp3 `Throughput` setting, sized to fit the instance's EBS limit.

### Why IOPS looks normal
- **Alarm:** `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` (VolumeReadBytes Sum per 60 s above 6e9, 3 of 3 datapoints, no actions configured) went to ALARM at 18:11:18 UTC. The breaching values were about 7.869e9 bytes/min, which is 125.07 MiB/s.
- **Since when:** the job came back at 18:07 UTC, two minutes after the instance was started at 18:05:10, and hit the cap at 18:08. So it has been throttled for about 85 minutes, not just the last half hour.
- **The arithmetic:** from 19:03 to 19:33 UTC the volume did only reads, at 125.07 MiB/s (range 125.06–125.08) and 500.3 IOPS, in 256 KiB requests. 500 IOPS × 256 KiB = 125 MiB/s. Large sequential reads hit the throughput cap while using only 17% of the 3,000 IOPS.
- **The volume's own check confirms it:** `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` was 1 in 87 of 88 minutes (18:07–19:33). `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` was 0 in all 88.
- **Requests are waiting:** queue length averaged 1.57, read latency 3.13 ms, and idle time 0.001%.
- **It's not a fault:** `VolumeStalledIOCheck` was 0 in all 88 minutes and the volume status is ok.

### Limits (19:03–19:33 UTC)

| Layer | Measured | Limit | Binds? |
|---|---|---|---|
| vol-0123456789abcdef0 IOPS | 500 IOPS | 3,000 IOPS | No |
| vol-0123456789abcdef0 throughput | 125.07 MiB/s | 125 MiB/s | **Yes** |
| io2 vol-1234567890abcdef0_4 | 985 IOPS, 7.7 MiB/s | 1,000 IOPS | Separate finding |
| gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 / root vol-1234567890abcdef0_20 | idle / 0.01 MiB/s | — | No |
| Instance c6i.xlarge (all 4 volumes) | 132.8 MiB/s, 1,488 IOPS | 156.25 MB/s = 149.01 MiB/s; 6,000 IOPS | No, about 16 MiB/s left |

- **The instance isn't the limit today:** both instance throttle checks were 0 in all 88 minutes, and the instance's EBS burst balances (`EBSByteBalance%` and `EBSIOBalance%`) stayed at 99%. CPU is about 1%.
- **It's a fixed ceiling, not a slowdown:** the job hit the same 125.07 MiB/s limit from 08:00 to 13:00 (throttled 60 of 60 minutes every hour) and from 16:23 to 17:24. Read latency held at about 3.0 ms throughout.
- **Nothing was changed:** the volume has never been modified, and CloudTrail shows no `ModifyVolume` calls in the last 24 hours. The instance was stopped at 17:17:43 and started at 18:05:10, with no instance type change.

### What to change
These are proposals; I haven't run anything. A typed approval in chat doesn't count. A change runs only when an operator approves it on the approval card, or you can run the commands yourself.

1. **Quick fix, online, no detach:**
   `aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 140 --region us-east-1`
   - How I got 140: the instance's 149.01 MiB/s limit minus 7.81 MiB/s used by the io2 volume and 0.02 MiB/s by the root volume leaves 141.18 MiB/s.
   - This gives only about 12% more, because the instance limit (149 MiB/s) becomes the next ceiling.
2. **For a real speedup:**
   - Change the instance to c6i.2xlarge. Its EBS limit is 312.5 MB/s = 298.02 MiB/s and 12,000 IOPS. This needs a stop/start, so do it between job runs.
   - Then set throughput to 290 MiB/s: `aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 290 --region us-east-1`. That's 298.02 − 7.81 − 0.02.
   - Keep IOPS at 3,000. gp3 allows up to 0.25 MiB/s per IOPS, so 3,000 IOPS supports up to 750 MiB/s.
   - If you need more later, c6i.4xlarge allows 596.05 MiB/s.
3. **Don't set 250–500 MiB/s on the current c6i.xlarge.** It would run fast only until the instance's burst balance drains, then all volumes together drop back to 149 MiB/s.
4. **Volume modification rules:** you can make up to 4 changes per volume in any 24 hours. There's no fixed wait between them; each one just has to finish first. All 4 are available now. The state goes modifying, then optimizing, then completed, and the new throughput already applies during optimizing.
   - To undo: `--throughput 125` once the change completes. That counts as one of the 4.
   - Throughput above 125 MiB/s costs extra, and a larger instance costs more. See the EBS and EC2 pricing pages.

### Other things I noticed
The io2 volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_4 is at its own 1,000 IOPS limit (985 average, 1,000.1 peak), and it shares the instance's EBS limit.

### What I couldn't check
- **The job's real demand is unknown.** It has been capped the whole time, so all I know is that it wants more than 125 MiB/s.
- **I didn't look inside the job.** I didn't check application or OS-level data for why it reads this way.
- **Some checks were skipped:** I didn't read the io2 volume's throttle checks, and I didn't check AWS Health or fault-injection experiments (AWS FIS). The data shows the job hitting a fixed limit rather than a fault, so they're unlikely to matter.

{"id": "916904a821bf43bfa8aa248f23cbd50b", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "The background Task subagent assigned to task "propose-mitigation" successfully completed:

## Results
I'm proposing an online change to gp3 volume `vol-0123456789abcdef0`: raise its throughput from 125 to 140 MiB/s. That's about a 12% gain for the batch job, the most this c6i.xlarge allows. The volume stays attached and the instance doesn't need a reboot. The plan passed the safety policy check with no violations, and nothing has been executed.

Getting the job materially faster for long runs takes a bigger instance: move to c6i.2xlarge, then set the volume to 290 MiB/s. That needs a stop/start, so it's planned downtime, and it isn't in the validated plan.

**Current state (account 012345678901_1, us-east-1):**
- **Volume:** `vol-0123456789abcdef0` is gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, in use as `/dev/sdg` on `i-1234567890abcdef0_5`.
- **No modification in progress:** the volume has no modification record, and the investigation counted no throughput or IOPS changes on it in the last 24h. All 4 of the allowed changes per rolling 24 hours are still available.
- **Instance limit:** `i-1234567890abcdef0_5` is a running c6i.xlarge. Its sustained EBS limit is 156.25 MB/s, which is 149.01 MiB/s, and 6,000 IOPS. Your EC2 API response shows `EbsOptimized: false`, but c6i is EBS-optimized by default, so the 149.01 MiB/s limit still applies.
- **Next size up:** c6i.2xlarge sustains 312.5 MB/s (298.02 MiB/s) and 12,000 IOPS.

**Why 140 MiB/s:** the instance can sustain 149.01 MiB/s across all its volumes. The io2 volume uses 7.81 MiB/s and the root volume 0.02 MiB/s, which leaves 141.18 MiB/s, so 140 MiB/s fits. After the change, the instance's 149.01 MiB/s becomes the next limit. Going higher on this instance (for example 250–500 MiB/s) would only last until the instance's EBS burst balance drains, then everything drops back to 149 MiB/s.

### Execution plan

**Prepare**
1. Save the current settings as your rollback reference:
   `aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}' > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json`
   You should see gp3, 20, 3000, 125, in-use.
2. Optionally, take a snapshot first:
   `aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "Pre-change backup before gp3 throughput 125->140" --region us-east-1`
   - The policy check suggested a backup. Changing throughput doesn't put data at risk, so this is just a safety measure.
   - Snapshot storage costs extra.

**Pre-validate**
3. Check that no modification is running:
   `aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1`
   You should get `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound`, or a latest state of `completed`. If it says `modifying` or `optimizing`, wait.

**Apply**
4. Raise the throughput:
   `aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 140 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1`
   - It runs online and uses 1 of the 4 changes allowed per 24 hours, leaving 3.
   - Each change must finish before the next one starts; there's no fixed wait beyond that.
   - The state goes `modifying` → `optimizing` → `completed`. The new throughput already applies during `optimizing`.
   - The volume costs more per month above the free 125 MiB/s (see https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/pricing/).

**Post-validate**
5. Confirm the new settings:
   `aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}'`
   You should see Throughput 140, Iops 3000, in-use.
6. Track the modification:
   `aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetThroughput:TargetThroughput,Progress:Progress}'`
7. About 10–15 minutes later, check that the job's read speed has gone up (Sum ÷ 60 ÷ 1,048,576 should approach 140 MiB/s):
   `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 --start-time <change time> --end-time <now> --region us-east-1`
   - Also check `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` (namespace AWS/EC2, `InstanceId=i-1234567890abcdef0_5`). It should stay at 0.
   - The alarm `example-b-gp3-read-bytes` fires above 6e9 bytes per minute, about 95.4 MiB/s. It will stay in ALARM at 140 MiB/s, because that's still above its threshold. Its OK state isn't a sign of success here; you may want to retune the threshold.

**Rollback**
8. Once the change reaches `optimizing` or `completed`, revert with:
   `aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1`
   This counts as another of the 4 changes allowed per 24 hours.

### Optional: c6i.2xlarge (not part of the validated plan)
Use this if 140 MiB/s isn't enough. It needs a maintenance window.
1. `aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_5 --region us-east-1`, then wait until the state is `stopped`.
2. `aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id i-1234567890abcdef0_5 --instance-type Value=c6i.2xlarge --region us-east-1`
3. `aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0_5 --region us-east-1`
4. Once the earlier change has finished, run `aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 290 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1`.
   - 290 = 298.02 − 7.81 − 0.02. 3000 IOPS supports up to 750 MiB/s on gp3, so IOPS can stay at 3000.
   - The next limit is c6i.2xlarge's 298.02 MiB/s. The size above, c6i.4xlarge, sustains 625 MB/s (596.05 MiB/s).

Before running this, check that nothing on the instance needs to keep running (patching tags are present; there's no Auto Scaling Group tag). To roll back, stop the instance, set the type back to c6i.xlarge, and start it again. Lower the volume to 140 or 125 MiB/s first. The instance costs more per hour.

### What a durable fix needs
- **Set the throughput where the volume is defined:** wherever `example-b-gp3-throughput` (`vol-0123456789abcdef0`) is managed, set throughput to 140 MiB/s, or 290 MiB/s together with c6i.2xlarge. That way a redeploy won't put it back to 125.
  - Done when that definition shows the throughput you chose.
  - And when applying it changes nothing on a volume that already has that value.
- **Size the volume and the instance together:** add a check that the sum of all volume throughput stays within the instance's sustained EBS limit (149.01 MiB/s on c6i.xlarge).
  - Done when a configuration that goes over that limit is flagged before deployment.

### What I could not cover
- **The job's real demand:** it's unknown, because its reads have been held at exactly 125 MiB/s. 140 MiB/s may not be enough, and the instance change may be needed.
- **Where the volume is defined:** I found no repository or pipeline for it, so the durable fix has no repository link.

The proposed change is a volume modification. Your EBS skill says it runs only as a directed action that an operator approves on the approval card; a typed "approve" in chat doesn't count. Otherwise, you can run the commands above with your own credentials.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Read-bytes alarm on gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** CloudWatch alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes ([redacted ARN]) went to ALARM at 2026-11-23 18:11:18 UTC. 3 of 3 datapoints of VolumeReadBytes (Sum, 60s) were above 6.0E9: 7.869E9 at 18:08, 7.869E9 at 18:09 and 7.869E9 at 18:10. The alarm has no actions configured.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T18:08:00Z

## Findings

### Root Cause: gp3 volume capped at provisioned 125 MiB/s throughput
**Description:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s, /dev/sdg on i-1234567890abcdef0_5, account 012345678901_1, us-east-1) is the binding limit. The batch job does pure sequential 256 KiB reads: 500 IOPS x 256 KiB = 125 MiB/s, so the volume reaches its throughput cap while using only 17% of its IOPS. VolumeThroughputExceededCheck was 1 in 87 of 88 minutes (18:07-19:33 UTC); VolumeIOPSExceededCheck, the instance throttle checks and VolumeStalledIOCheck were all 0. Queue length averaged 1.57, read latency 3.13 ms, idle time ~0%. The same fixed ceiling held 08:00-13:00 and 16:23-17:24. Not a fault: volume status ok, no modifications or ModifyVolume calls. The instance (c6i.xlarge, 149.01 MiB/s EBS limit) is not binding today, with 132.8 MiB/s used across all volumes and burst balances at 99%, but it is the next ceiling.
**Cascades to:** symptom-gp3-read-bytes-alarm

#### Supporting Observations
- **Volume is gp3 at baseline 3000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (example-b-gp3-throughput, Scenario b) is a 20 GiB gp3 volume with 3000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s throughput, attached as /dev/sdg to i-1234567890abcdef0_5 in us-east-1a. About 7.87 GB/min works out to ~131 MB/s (~125 MiB/s), so the reads are at the volume's provisioned throughput ceiling. Other attached volumes: io2 vol-1234567890abcdef0_4 (/dev/sdf), gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 (/dev/sdi, 200 GiB) and the root volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_20.
- **VolumeThroughputExceededCheck = 1 continuously since 18:07:** For vol-0123456789abcdef0 on i-1234567890abcdef0_5, VolumeThroughputExceededCheck (1-min Maximum) was 0 at 18:06, then 1 in every minute from 18:07 to 19:33 UTC (87 of 88 datapoints). VolumeIOPSExceededCheck stayed at 0, and so did InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck, InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeStalledIOCheck. The volume's throughput limit is being hit. The IOPS limit, the instance's limits and stalled I/O are not.
- **Workload is pure sequential 256 KiB reads at a flat 125.07 MiB/s:** 19:03–19:34 UTC on vol-0123456789abcdef0: throughput 125.06–125.08 MiB/s (flat), ~500 IOPS, average I/O size exactly 256 KiB, zero writes. VolumeQueueLength averaged 1.57 (max 3.6), read latency ~3.1 ms/op (max 7.2), and idle time was ~0%, so the volume is saturated. At 256 KiB per I/O, 125 MiB/s works out to ~500 IOPS, far below the 3000 IOPS provisioned.
- **Instance EBS burst balances stay at 99%:** i-1234567890abcdef0_5, 19:03–19:34 UTC: EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% held at a minimum of 99%, and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck and InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck stayed at 0. Instance-level EBS bandwidth is not the bottleneck. Other volumes: io2 vol-1234567890abcdef0_4 averaged ~985 IOPS (1000 provisioned) at ~7.7 MiB/s. gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 was idle. The root volume showed negligible I/O.
- **Volume has repeatedly hit its 125 MiB/s limit since 07:00 UTC:** Hourly view for Nov 23: throughput averaged 125.07 MiB/s every hour from 08:00 to 12:00 UTC, with the throughput limit exceeded all 60 minutes of each hour. The volume was idle 14:00–15:59. Reads resumed at 16:00 (84 MiB/s average; limit exceeded 41 of 60 minutes), then ran 17:00 (18 min), 18:00 (53 min) and 19:00 (35 min). Peak 1-minute throughput was ~125.1 MiB/s in every active hour, meaning the ceiling is hard. Read latency stayed at ~3 ms/op throughout.
- **No volume config changes; instance stopped 17:17 and started 18:05:** CloudTrail (2026-11-22T19:30Z–2026-11-23T19:35Z) shows no events for vol-0123456789abcdef0, and describe_volumes_modifications shows the volume has never been modified. The only write events on i-1234567890abcdef0_5 were StopInstances at 17:17:43 UTC and StartInstances at 18:05:10 UTC, both by user example-session. The read workload stopped with the instance and resumed right after the start. No configuration change explains the alarm, so the reads come from workload demand.
- **All 4 attached volumes report status ok:** describe_volume_status reports io-enabled passed and io-performance normal for vol-0123456789abcdef0, vol-1234567890abcdef0_4, vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 and vol-1234567890abcdef0_20. No events or actions are scheduled. No volume modification history was found.

#### Gaps
- **Job's true throughput demand unknown:** The job has been capped at 125 MiB/s the whole time, so its real demand is unknown beyond exceeding 125 MiB/s. Application and OS-level data were not examined.

## Other Gaps

### io2 throttle checks, AWS Health and FIS not checked
**Description:** The io2 volume's throttle checks, AWS Health events, and AWS FIS experiments were not reviewed. These are unlikely to matter because the data shows a fixed limit rather than a fault.

### Volume's IaC/pipeline source not found
**Description:** No repository or pipeline defining example-b-gp3-throughput (vol-0123456789abcdef0) was found, so the durable throughput change has no repository link and a redeploy could revert it to 125 MiB/s.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise gp3 throughput on vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 125 to 140 MiB/s (online, no detach)

## Reasoning
The volume is pinned at its 125 MiB/s throughput while using only ~500 of 3,000 IOPS. The c6i.xlarge sustains 149.01 MiB/s of EBS traffic across all volumes; minus 7.81 MiB/s (io2) and 0.02 MiB/s (root), 141.18 MiB/s is left, so 140 MiB/s fits (~12% gain). Above that, the instance becomes the cap once its burst balance drains. For a material speedup, move to c6i.2xlarge (298.02 MiB/s) and set 290 MiB/s; that needs a stop/start and is outside the validated plan. The plan passed the safety policy check; nothing has been executed. The change runs only after operator approval on the approval card.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Record current settings as the rollback reference (expect gp3, 20…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}' > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json
```
**Purpose:** Record current settings as the rollback reference (expect gp3, 20, 3000, 125, in-use)

#### 1.2 Optionally snapshot the volume before changing it
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "Pre-change backup before gp3 throughput 125->140" --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Optionally snapshot the volume before changing it
**Advisory:** Throughput changes do not put data at risk; this is a precaution suggested by the policy check, Snapshot storage costs extra

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Ensure the volume is free to modify (expect…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Ensure the volume is free to modify (expect InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound or completed; wait if modifying/optimizing)

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Lift the gp3 throughput cap online without detaching
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 140 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Lift the gp3 throughput cap online without detaching
**Risks:** Uses 1 of 4 modifications allowed per rolling 24 h
**Advisory:** Throughput above 125 MiB/s is billed extra (https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/pricing/), New throughput applies already during the optimizing state

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm Throughput 140, Iops 3000, in-use
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State}'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm Throughput 140, Iops 3000, in-use

#### 4.2 Track the modification through modifying, optimizing, completed
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetThroughput:TargetThroughput,Progress:Progress}'
```
**Purpose:** Track the modification through modifying, optimizing, completed

#### 4.3 Check after 10 to 15 min that read rate approaches 140 MiB/s (Sum / 60…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeReadBytes --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Sum --period 60 --start-time <change time> --end-time <now> --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Check after 10 to 15 min that read rate approaches 140 MiB/s (Sum / 60 / 1048576)
**Advisory:** Also confirm AWS/EC2 InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck for i-1234567890abcdef0_5 stays 0, Alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes (6e9 B/min ~ 95.4 MiB/s) will stay in ALARM at 140 MiB/s; it is not a success signal, so consider retuning it

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Restore the original throughput once the change reaches optimizing or…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Restore the original throughput once the change reaches optimizing or completed
**Risks:** Counts as another of the 4 modifications allowed per 24 h

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Codify the new throughput where the volume is defined
**Description:** Wherever example-b-gp3-throughput (vol-0123456789abcdef0) is managed, set throughput to 140 MiB/s, or 290 MiB/s together with c6i.2xlarge, so a redeploy does not revert it to 125.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The volume definition shows the chosen throughput
- Applying the definition changes nothing on a volume already at that value

#### 2. Size volume and instance throughput together
**Description:** Add a check that the sum of attached volume throughput stays within the instance's sustained EBS limit (149.01 MiB/s on c6i.xlarge).
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- A configuration exceeding the instance's sustained EBS limit is flagged before deployment

     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"
     23	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Operations
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs, unless the user gives the values and asks you to treat them as given (see Critical Rules). Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window. For a performance verdict, include the side-by-side limits table from [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#limits-table-for-performance-verdicts) and the recent history (alarm history, modification history, earlier occurrences of the same pattern).
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation:
     96	
     97	- Only the recorded symptoms, findings, observations and gaps reach the investigation summary. Text in a chat message or a later mitigation plan does not, so put the verdict and the recommendation in the findings.
     98	- Write the symptom with its impact: the alarm name, threshold and breaching datapoints, whether the alarm has actions, and the onset time.
     99	- Write the root cause finding description as a complete answer on its own, in this order:
     100	  1. "Binding layer: `<layer>`." in those words.
     101	  2. The numbers that prove it: the exceeded checks (minutes at 1), per-volume demand against the volume limit, and the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes against the instance EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, for example "500 IOPS x 256 KiB = 125 MiB/s, the provisioned throughput".
     102	  3. The recent history: alarm episodes, modification history, and whether earlier peaks stopped at the same ceiling.
     103	  4. "Recommendation (proposal, not executed; it runs only after an operator approves it on the approval card):" the exact command with the target, how the target was computed, the next limit after the change, and the EBS baseline of the next larger instance size when the instance becomes the next limit.
     104	  Do not leave the conclusion or the target only under Gaps or in a later message.
     105	- Record each piece of evidence as an observation and link every observation that supports a finding to it, so each finding shows its supporting observations. This includes the limits table, the instance layer check, the volume status result and the history.
     106	- Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding. Leave out AWS FIS experiments, AWS CloudTrail events and alarms on resources that are not attached to the instance.
     107	- Link a gap only to the findings it affects. Record a gap that applies to the whole answer once.
     108	
     109	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, keep it as the verdict and write "Binding layer: Indeterminate" with the answer to the user's question first. Then present a short list of candidate causes, as described in [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#indeterminate-candidate-causes). For each candidate, give the supporting observations with numbers and the specific check that would confirm it or rule it out. Merge overlapping candidates, and name a candidate that the data rules out as ruled out, with the numbers. Do not name AWS-side impairment as the cause, and do not call the pattern an impairment pattern. Give the customer the detailed performance statistics step from [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) to run during the symptom.
     110	
     111	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     112	
     113	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     114	
     115	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     116	
     117	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     118	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The answer says "Binding layer:" followed by the layer, and gives the four exceeded checks as minutes at 1 or "no datapoints". A performance verdict has the limits table: per-volume demand next to the volume limit, summed demand of all attached volumes next to the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS, which one binds, and the exact target with its computation.
     119	- A performance verdict states the recent history: the alarm history, the modification history (latest record and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or a Gap), and whether the same pattern happened earlier.
     120	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     121	- An Indeterminate verdict says "Binding layer: Indeterminate", answers the user's question first, and lists the candidate causes, each with its supporting observations and the check that confirms or rules it out, without overlapping candidates or the same gap repeated under each one.
     122	- In an investigation, the root cause finding (or, for Indeterminate, the first finding) carries the verdict, the numbers, the history and the Recommendation, because only findings reach the summary.
     123	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first. The first lines of a snapshot answer name every snapshot with its tier and the evidence for it.
     124	- Every proposed change follows [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals): exact command, expected effect, modifications left in the 24-hour window, rollback, and the approval statement.
     125	- When a volume modification is in progress, the answer states the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window, each one completing before the next, and the count used from AWS CloudTrail or a Gap.
     126	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     127	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     128	
     129	---
     130	
     131	## Critical Rules
     132	
     133	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, key changes, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval, and the reply says so in those words whenever the user types an approval. Each proposal also gives the exact AWS CLI command the customer can run with their own credentials. See [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals).
     134	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     135	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first. Do not end the turn with a question tool or a request to pick a value: give the recommended proposal, and the command for any value the user named, then say the user can choose.
     136	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     137	- **Given facts stay given.** When the user supplies the values and asks you to treat them as given, reason from those values only. Do not query the account for other resources, and do not mix account data into the given facts. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs.
     138	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     139	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     140	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     141	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     142	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     143	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. State this rule in the answer whenever a modification is in progress or proposed.
     144	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     145	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     146	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     147	
     148	## Gotchas
     149	
     150	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     151	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     152	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     153	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     154	- When the instance is the binding layer, do not call the volume saturated, even when its idle time is near 0. Say that its I/O is waiting on the instance limit.
     155	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     156	- `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`, `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, and no datapoints is not the same as 0. The instance checks `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with `InstanceId`.
     157	- Amazon EBS detailed performance statistics are read on the instance, not through an AWS API. They are a step the customer runs; the agent never runs them.
     158	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     159	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     160	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     161	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     162	
     163	## Error Handling
     164	
     165	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     166
